the_story: Indian government bonds (debt papers issued by the state to borrow money) saw slight price gains because of an upward trend in US Treasuries (bonds issued by the US government).
Investors are closely watching the upcoming weekly debt auction, which is a key event for how these markets move.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI, the country's central bank) might consider further rate hikes (raising the benchmark interest rate) because of retail inflation (rising prices of everyday goods in shops) and fluctuating oil prices.
analysis.what_happened: Prices of Indian government bonds rose slightly, copying a similar positive move in US government bonds. However, traders are holding back a bit because the government is about to sell a fresh batch of debt, and people are worried about inflation and changing oil prices which might cause the Reserve Bank of India to raise interest rates.
analysis.analogy: It is like when a popular coffee shop in the neighborhood raises its prices, the smaller cafe next door feels confident enough to nudge its prices up a little bit too, but only if regular customers keep showing up.
why_it_matters_india: US bond prices go up -> Indian bond prices follow the positive global mood and tick higher
The Indian government plans to sell more debt at a weekly auction -> This extra supply slows down how fast bond prices can rise
Retail inflation and shifting oil prices stay in play -> The Reserve Bank of India might think about raising interest rates
Traders watch all these moving pieces cautiously -> This hesitation affects how easily money flows in local financial markets

items.title: India's wheat area set for steepest decline in 26 years as farmers switch crops
items.summary: India is experiencing its most severe decline in wheat acreage in 26 years due to insufficient monsoon rains. Farmers are shifting to less water-intensive crops like chickpeas and rapeseed, which promise better returns. The government's minimal increase in wheat procurement prices has also discouraged wheat planting among farmers. As a result, wheat acreage is expected to drop to its lowest level in four years.

items.title: India's wheat area set for biggest drop in 26 years as farmers switch crops
items.summary: Weak monsoon and El Niño spur shift to chickpeas, rapeseed; planting down 15.3% so far

items.title: India's wheat area set for biggest drop in 26 years as farmers switch crops
items.summary: Weak monsoon and El Niño spur shift to chickpeas, rapeseed; planting down 15.3% so far

items.title: India wheat area set for biggest drop in 26 years as farmers switch crops | 104 . 1 WIKY

events.article_text:
India's main winter-sown crop, wheat usually competes for acreage with rapeseed, chickpeas and corn (Photo: PTI)

India's wheat acreage is poised for its steepest decline in 26 years as fields parched by the weakest monsoon rains in more than a decade spur farmers ​to switch to competing crops in search of better returns, industry officials told ​Reuters.

The drop in planting, coupled with the risk of lower yields brought by a severe El Niño ‌weather pattern, threatens to curb output in the world's second-largest wheat producer, in turn boosting prices and complicating efforts to damp food inflation.

"Wheat needs to be irrigated at least four to five times, but we don't have enough water even to sow the crop," said farmer Vilas Bhutekar in the Jalna district of the western state of Maharashtra.

"So we chose chickpeas instead, as they require less water."

India's June-September monsoon rains were the lowest in more than a decade as the drying effect of the El Niño drove rainfall as much as 41 per cent below average in key wheat-growing states such as Punjab, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.

"Wheat needs more water than other competing ‌crops," said Nitin Gupta, deputy country head at agricultural trader Olam Agri India.

"But water is in short supply in some regions this year, which could mean farmers plant less wheat."

Wheat was planted across 5 million hectares (12 million acres) by Nov. 13, down 15.3 per cent from a year earlier, government data show.

Planting for the 2026/27 season is expected to fall about 6 per cent from last year's record of 33.6 million hectares (83 million acres), an average estimate by 10 industry officials shows.

That would be the steepest decline since 2000/01, taking area under the crop to the lowest ​in four years at 31.58 million hectares (78 million acres).

Wheat acreage is expected to stay largely steady in the key ‌northern states of Haryana and Punjab, which have access to reliable irrigation.

But farmers in other states are likely to shift from wheat to less-thirsty crops such as chickpea and rapeseed, industry officials said.

Prices of these crops ​have risen much ‌more than wheat, prompting farmers to shift acreage away from the grain, said Sandeep Bansal, director of a flour miller ‌based in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh.

"Wheat is usually farmers' first choice, but this year other crops are giving better returns," Bansal said.

The state-run Food Corporation of India buys wheat from farmers at the minimum ‌support ​price, which New ​Delhi raised this year by just 1 per cent to 2,610 rupees per 100 kg, the smallest increase since 2002/03.

"The government typically incentivises wheat planting by raising procurement prices by 5 to 6 per cent annually," said ‌a New Delhi-based trader ​with a global trade house.

"This year's 1 per cent hike is, in fact, discouraging farmers from expanding wheat acreage."

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

analysis.tldr: A sharp drop in wheat planting due to water shortages and low government price hikes means higher food prices and a tougher battle against inflation for everyday households.
the_story: India's wheat acreage is heading for its biggest drop in 26 years, with planting expected to fall about 6% to 31.58 million hectares for the 2026/27 season.

The decline is driven by the weakest monsoon rains in over a decade—caused by the El Niño weather pattern—which left key states like Punjab, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Maharashtra with up to 41% below-average rainfall.
Farmers are switching from water-heavy wheat to less-thirsty, more profitable competing crops like chickpeas and rapeseed.

Government support: New Delhi raised the minimum support price (the guaranteed price the government pays farmers) by just 1% to 2,610 rupees per 100 kg, the smallest increase since 2002/03, which discourages wheat expansion.
Government data shows wheat was planted across 5 million hectares by Nov. 13, down 15.3% from a year earlier.
analysis.what_happened: Monsoon rains hit a ten-year low because of the El Niño weather pattern (a natural climate cycle that warms ocean waters and dries out rainfall). This left fields parched and reservoirs short on water. Because wheat needs four to five rounds of watering—much more than other crops—and the government offered a tiny 1% price hike for it, farmers chose to plant thriftier, better-paying crops like chickpeas instead.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local bakery owner deciding to bake fewer loaves of bread because flour costs too much water to make, and customers are willing to pay a lot more for cookies instead—leaving fewer loaves on the shelf for everyone else.
why_it_matters_india: Weak monsoon and dry fields reduce the amount of land used for wheat farming.
Lower wheat planting threatens to curb total crop output in India, the world's second-largest wheat producer.
Fewer crops mean scarcer supplies, which pushes up food prices and worsens food inflation.
Hotter food inflation forces the central bank to keep interest rates higher for longer, making everyday loans costlier for households.

impacts.rationale: Scarcity of a major food grain like wheat pushes grocery bills higher, which is bad for household budgets.

impacts.target: Wheat and food prices in India
impacts.rationale: Lower production and reduced planting directly translate to costlier food staples—bad for consumers.

watch_next: Government announcements on wheat stock releases or import policies
Winter weather and any unseasonal rain patterns affecting the surviving crops
analysis.caveats: If unexpected winter rains arrive to help parched fields, the final crop yield drop might not be as severe as currently feared.

items.title: Hormuz Oil Exports Could Decline amid Inbound Tanker Shortage
items.summary: Analysts are touting the remarkable recovery in crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf, which have jumped close to pre-war levels in recent months. events.article_text:
Senate Passes Sweeping Energy Permitting Reform Bill in 62-33 Vote

What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,…

Analysts are touting the remarkable recovery in crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf, which have jumped close to pre-war levels in recent months.

The oil market reflects the bearish sentiment, with Brent Crude prices sliding in the past weeks to around $92 per barrel, down from a recent peak of over $118 per barrel in late October.

The market and most analysts assume that the steady flow of crude oil from the Strait of Hormuz and the entire Middle Eastern region will continue into the next months, rebalancing supply and demand and even tipping the balance into a large surplus next year.

However, in the volatile situation in and around the Strait of Hormuz, with no recent rapprochement for potential U.S.-Iran talks, nothing is given, and no forecast has more than 50/50 odds of panning out.

The Iran war has reshuffled trade routes and patterns and tied up more tankers in inefficient and lengthy voyages.

The increased flows of oil from the Strait of Hormuz, mostly thanks to ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, are tying up supertankers for weeks waiting for the transfers outside the Strait, limiting the availability of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) for the other global key oil trade routes, such as the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia.

The inefficient shuttle shipping is tying up a growing number of smaller vessels, Suezmaxes and Aframaxes, too, on the Hormuz trade.

This leaves fewer available empty tankers globally willing to travel to the Middle East to pick up cargoes in the Gulf of Oman.

The total capacity of the empty tankers going to the Middle East has slumped by some 40% since the end of August, per data from Tankertrackers.com cited by Bloomberg.

There are “not enough vacant tankers to take oil out of the region,” Tankertrackers.com’s co-founder, Samir Madani, told the publication.

“It’s one thing to bring the oil out into the Gulf of Oman via the Strait of Hormuz, but it seems like there isn’t enough to take the oil out of the Gulf of Oman,” the analyst said.

As of November 16, the combined capacity of ballasting supertankers and Suezmaxes en route to the Gulf of Oman has slumped to 71 million barrels, down from 130 million barrels capacity at the end of August, according to data compiled by Tankertrackers.com.

To be sure, flows from the Middle East remain elevated, albeit somewhat lower so far in November compared to October. Crude oil exports from the Strait of Hormuz have held so far despite the worst month for attacks on tankers in the area since the war began.

The high crude oil export levels despite increased security risks give the market and many analysts confidence that the only path forward is continuous recovery and, ultimately, an oil glut within months.

Tanker rates have dropped from the record highs seen in early October, but they remain above historical norms and pre-war levels amid heightened war insurance premiums and security risks.

“Security risks continue to weigh on tanker operations in the Gulf,” Maria Bertzeletou, Senior Market Analyst at Signal Group, wrote in an analysis this week.

“Repeated attacks continue to restrict the pool of owners willing to accept Gulf employment, while elevated war-risk insurance costs and operational delays add to voyage expenses and limit effective vessel availability.”

So far this month, Iran has been reporting nearly daily incidents of tankers hitting naval mines in corridors that Iran has designated as “unauthorized” in the Strait of Hormuz.

Non-Iranian observers and organizations also report more frequent attacks on tankers in and near the Strait of Hormuz.

Five tankers have been struck near Hormuz in the week between November 11 and 18, according to remote-sensing intelligence by Windward.

“This highlights Iran’s continued strategy of maritime attrition, and it is unlikely to ease unless diplomatic conditions change,” the maritime intelligence firm said on Wednesday.

Despite the threat to tanker shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, investment banks and the International Energy Agency (IEA) expect the crude oil market to be in a surplus as early as this quarter.

“We continue to expect the oil balance to loosen as supply recovers, limiting the scope for a sustained rebound in prices,” ING’s commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in a Wednesday note.

In its November monthly report, the IEA said that the global oil market will return to a surplus this quarter, with a more substantial build in 2027.

“As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery,” the agency noted.

Goldman Sachs Research’s latest forecast calls for oil prices easing gradually in 2027 as suppliers in the Middle East adapt to disruption from the war in Iran.

Goldman’s commodities analysts expect Brent Crude to average $88 per barrel in 2027 under their base case assumption of no definitive diplomatic breakthrough in Iran and no re-escalation with major long-term damage to oil infrastructure.

Under the same base case scenario, Goldman Sachs forecasts that Brent will fall from around $92 per barrel today to $78 by early December 2027 “as a sizable surplus decreases Brent’s fair value from $90 per barrel today to the high $70s by the end of 2027.”

analysis.tldr: A shortage of empty oil tankers heading to the Middle East could disrupt crude oil flows, which might eventually drive up fuel prices in India.
the_story: Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf have recently jumped close to pre-war levels, pushing Brent Crude prices down to around $92 per barrel from a late October peak of over $118.
However, ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman are tying up supertankers for weeks, cutting the total capacity of empty tankers heading to the Middle East by about 40% since the end of August.

Data from Tankertrackers.com shows the combined capacity of ballasting supertankers and Suezmaxes en route to the Gulf of Oman dropped from 130 million barrels at the end of August to 71 million barrels by November 16.

Ongoing security risks, high war-risk insurance costs, and frequent attacks on tankers—including five tankers struck near the Strait of Hormuz between November 11 and 18—continue to restrict the number of shipowners willing to operate in the region.

Despite these maritime threats, organizations like the International Energy Agency (IEA) and investment banks like Goldman Sachs still expect global oil markets to enter a surplus, potentially pushing Brent Crude down to $78 by early December 2027.
analysis.what_happened: Oil exports from the Middle East have recovered, but inefficient shipping routes and ship-to-ship transfers are trapping large oil tankers (supertankers) in long waits. At the same time, ongoing attacks and high war-insurance costs in the Strait of Hormuz are making fewer empty tankers willing to travel to the region to pick up oil, creating a severe shortage of available transport vessels.
analysis.analogy: It is like a delivery hub where trucks are getting stuck waiting too long to unload, leaving delivery companies with too few empty trucks to go back and pick up new goods.
why_it_matters_india: Fewer available tankers in the Middle East -> Risk of oil transport bottlenecks
Transport bottlenecks or supply disruptions -> Potential pressure on global crude oil prices
Costlier crude oil for India -> Higher import bills and a weaker rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars)
Higher import costs -> Increased domestic inflation and costlier fuel for everyday Indians

impacts.rationale: If tanker shortages disrupt oil flows and push crude prices up, fuel prices for everyday consumers could rise, which is bad for household budgets.
Costlier oil imports force India to buy more dollars to pay for energy, weakening the rupee—which makes imported goods more expensive for regular people.
More expensive fuel and transport raise the cost of everyday goods across India, reducing household purchasing power.

watch_next: Data updates on empty tanker capacity heading to the Middle East
Reports of further attacks or security incidents in the Strait of Hormuz
analysis.caveats: Even with severe tanker shortages, major institutions like the IEA and Goldman Sachs expect overall oil supplies to grow into a surplus, which could keep prices heading downward instead.

events.headline: The Ground Beneath the Cloud: Dispersion and Dependency in the Digital Age

items.title: The Ground Beneath the Cloud: Dispersion and Dependency in the Digital Age
items.summary: Commercial cloud architecture has made digital infrastructure more resilient to localized disruption. Geographic dispersion, workload migration, and failover have allowed providers to preserve access in instances of degradation or even destruction. Yet, underpinning this resiliency are interlocking dependencies on access to energy, supply chains, and governing bodies that extend well beyond the data centers hosting the commercial cloud. The United States is building digital capacity — data centers and the underlying systems supporting them — faster than the governance frameworks needed to orch

events.article_text:
A year ago, I wrote about data centers as the decisive infrastructure of the 21st century, exposed and unaccounted for in real doctrine. Frameworks like the Pentagon’s Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability and its emerging successor, the Unified Cloud Marketplace­, established requirements for providers to disperse workloads across data centers hundreds of miles apart and build failover into their contracts, while the Pentagon diversifies across commercial hyperscale providers. This framework should grow to encompass the rapid expansion of infrastructure that threatens to leave behind the geographic dispersion needed to protect data survivability.

Writing for Cogs of War in July of this year, Blake Herzinger made the strongest case yet for what digital strategic depth should look like in protecting digital assets with his three pillars: dispersion, elasticity, and optionality — engineered so that a workload can survive an attack on any single point. He cites two recent cases. In Ukraine, critical workloads were moved onto allied territory cloud infrastructure during wartime, demonstrating how geographic dispersion can preserve access to data even when domestic infrastructure is under attack. When Iran struck Amazon Web Services facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain earlier this year — the first confirmed kinetic attack on public commercial cloud infrastructure — it demonstrated the scale of commercial cloud architecture where customers failed over into other regions. However, strategic depth bought this way is resilience temporarily rented. The cloud that had provided Bahrain a “cloud first” solution could not provide security independent of the physical infrastructure itself.

In September, Amazon made that distinction concrete: Amazon Web Services announced it could no longer restore access to resources and data hosted exclusively in its Bahrain region, after physical damage spread across multiple availability zones and exceeded what its regional and multi-availability zone architecture was “designed to withstand.” In the United Arab Emirates, Amazon Web Services made the same determination for one of three availability zones while recovery efforts continue in the other two. The dispersion that mitigated the initial strike could not indefinitely outrun the physical damage on the ground.

Hyperscalers would counter that multi-region failover, capacity planning, and supply chain management are their core business and that they do it better than any government could. Bahrain, they would add, is one attack with customers moving workloads to other regions as designed. But what happens when multiple regions — including the failover regions — are subject to multi-theater conflict? Customers’ failover into regions is dependent on strained transmission access and the same fiber, supply chains, and host governments, none of which a hyperscale provider controls.

Failover regions do not guarantee operational independence. In June 2025, a single faulty update crashed Google Cloud’s policy-checking system in every region of Google Cloud — one of the Pentagon’s four Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability providers — within seconds. The crash disrupted Google Cloud and Google Workspace services worldwide. Global physical links share similar characteristics as single points of failure. Subsea cables in the Persian Gulf that include Asia-Africa-Europe 1, FALCON, and the Gulf Bridge System run through the Strait of Hormuz. In October 2026, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters that Tehran has drawn up plans to target the Gulf’s undersea cables if the United States and Israel resume attacks, adding that Iran would aim to prevent repairs to prolong disruption. Moving a workload to another region does not remove it from these shared dependencies on the ground.

Is bigger better? A larger and more geographically distributed data center footprint means more substations, transmission lines, and fiber optic routes over land and sea, all of which fall on the state to protect as the scaling continues. Dispersion compounds nearly every constraint on scaling, from security and energy to space and resources.

Every new site needs new transmission, and transmission is currently on backorder. The Department of Energy’s July 2026 transmission study identified data centers as a major source of new load and found an urgent need for more transmission capacity. The International Energy Agency estimates that grid constraints alone could delay roughly 20 percent of global data center capacity planned through 2030. The backup queue continues to grow unabated, further distancing the goals of wider scaling.

Backup queues seem to be consistent outside the United States as well. In Brazil, data centers can be built in two years, while transmission lines to power them can take five to seven years to construct. In Chile, the constraints are seen in water availability. Google’s Quilicura Facility used roughly 461 million liters of water in 2024 amidst an ongoing — now over a decade-long — drought where every new site puts more pressure on availability. Across Europe, developers are moving farther away from major cities as power and land become scarce. This is affecting data center development not only going into the 2030s, but right now, as seen in Microsoft’s recently cancelled 50-megawatt data center lease in the United Kingdom due to grid connection delays.

New data centers need new hardware to function that’s already becoming scarce. Utilities are competing for transformers, breakers, and switchgear, with some high-voltage transformer lead times exceeding 160 weeks. Expansion is straining supplies of critical minerals and rare earths whose geographic concentration and refinement reside primarily in China.

Concentrated control of critical minerals gives Beijing leverage over data center development. Data center demand for gallium alone could reach 10 percent of global supply by 2030, while China produces 9

analysis.tldr: Global digital infrastructure faces severe physical bottlenecks and security threats, which can ripple into higher costs for tech services and delayed expansion for digital infrastructure globally.
the_story: Amazon Web Services could not restore access to resources hosted exclusively in its Bahrain region after physical damage exceeded its regional design, following an earlier strike by Iran.
A single faulty update in June 2025 crashed Google Cloud's policy-checking system worldwide within seconds, highlighting shared single points of failure.
The International Energy Agency estimates that electrical grid constraints could delay roughly 20 percent of global data center capacity planned through 2030.
China produces critical minerals and rare earths, and data center demand for gallium alone could reach 10 percent of global supply by 2030, giving Beijing leverage.
analysis.what_happened: Digital cloud infrastructure providers like Amazon and Google are facing severe physical limits, ranging from military attacks on facilities in the Middle East to global software crashes and a severe shortage of power grids, water, and hardware components like transformers.
analysis.analogy: It is like building a fleet of advanced digital delivery trucks, but realizing there are not enough paved roads, fuel stations, or spare parts to keep them running smoothly.
why_it_matters_india: Global cloud providers facing infrastructure bottlenecks and hardware shortages struggle to expand capacity at previous speeds.
Higher global competition for critical hardware, rare earths, and power transmission equipment drives up costs for digital infrastructure.
Indian companies relying heavily on global cloud services could face higher operational costs or capacity constraints.
Tech and IT service providers may need to spend more on building resilience against physical and digital disruptions.

impacts.target: IT stocks like TCS, Infosys & Wipro
impacts.rationale: Higher cloud infrastructure costs and global tech bottlenecks can squeeze margins for software service providers — generally bad for stock performance.
Scarcity of power equipment, hardware, and critical minerals drives up global tech and energy costs, making goods and services pricier for ordinary people — bad for consumers.

watch_next: Updates on global cloud provider stability and regional failover capabilities
Availability and lead times for electrical grid hardware like transformers
analysis.caveats: The article focuses heavily on global military, geographic, and grid constraints, so the direct financial impact on Indian retail investors depends heavily on corporate earnings reports.

events.headline: El Niño could deepen Tamil Nadu’s water stress and threaten agriculture

items.title: El Niño could deepen Tamil Nadu’s water stress and threaten agriculture
items.summary: Climate change induced global warming is significantly increasing baseline ocean temperatures and worsening the impacts of the naturally occurring El Niño cycle. The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) recently confirmed an 80-100% probability of the persistent El Niño phase extending to April 2027. For regions like India which are already climate stressed, […]

events.article_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Climate change induced global warming is significantly increasing baseline ocean temperatures and worsening the impacts of the naturally occurring El Niño cycle. The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) recently confirmed an 80-100% probability of the persistent El Niño phase extending to April 2027.

For regions like India which are already climate stressed, this El Niño can have a multiplier effect, exacerbating existing vulnerabilities. India experienced 16 El Niño events between 1951 and 2025 and they last generally for nine to 18 months. This year’s El Niño is projected to be severe and its impacts can already be seen in the form of extreme droughts or excess rainfall.

The southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu is staring at an acute water stress as it is already impacted on various fronts due to climate change. According to a 52-year climate study conducted between 1971 and 2022 published in International Journal of Climatology, the south peninsular region of India, including Tamil Nadu, is prone to drought. The study highlights that Tamil Nadu’s drought risk is a long-term trend.

Tamil Nadu depends on inflows from the southwest monsoon to replenish its reservoirs and rainfall from the northeast monsoon season for its water security. The southwest monsoon occurs between June and September and the northeast monsoon occurs between October and December. El Niño has the potential to influence rainfall including the northeast monsoon.

According to recent India Meteorological Department (IMD) data, this year’s southwest monsoon season ended on September 30 with a 12.6% rainfall deficiency which is the lowest since 2015. This creates rainfall deficit especially over the catchment areas in the Western Ghats affecting reservoir inflows to Tamil Nadu. The northeast monsoon officially started on October 15, and more clarity about the season is expected in the coming weeks.

While not all El Niño years result in drought, India’s major drought years happened during the El Niño years of 1982, 1987, 2002, 2009, and 2015. During strong El Niño years, Tamil Nadu experiences prolonged dry spells, deficient rainfall, temperature rise, depletion of reservoirs and a delayed onset of seasonal rains. In 2015, the southwest monsoon had a 14.3% rainfall deficiency; it was 21.8% deficient in 2009 and 19.2% in 2002.

The northeast monsoon season for 2026 officially started on October 15 and according to the projections by the Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU), Tamil Nadu is set to receive a normal rainfall of 468 mm compared to the seasonal average of 464 mm. Though this can provide partial relief, El Niño can cause variable rainfall distribution, where coastal districts may experience intense rainfall and interior districts may see more dry conditions, the TNAU forecast notes.

Agriculture in Tamil Nadu depends largely on the monsoon seasons and an uneven distribution of these monsoons makes rainfed farming systems more vulnerable, as reduced rainfall limits irrigation water, reduces moisture and consequently decreases crop yields. Major crops such as paddy, groundnut, maize, cotton, pulses, sugarcane, millets and coconut yields are affected. Livestock is also affected due to water stress and fodder shortages.

“Tamil Nadu benefits significantly from the northeast monsoon, and El Niño conditions can, in general, enhance northeast monsoon rainfall over the state. The El Niño year of 2015 is one such example,” says Akshay Deoras, a senior research scientist at the National Centre for Atmospheric Science and Department of Meteorology, University of Reading. “There are some early indications that rainfall along coastal Tamil Nadu could improve during November and December.”

Districts across Tamil Nadu have been flagged for El Niño vulnerabilities with a majority of these districts falling in the northern and central regions of Tamil Nadu including Ariyalur, Perambalur, Tiruppattur, Vellore, Tiruchirappalli, Cuddalore, Kallakurichi, Kanchipuram, Ranipettai, Tiruvallur, Tiruvannamalai, Villupuram and Pudukkottai. Many of these districts are agriculture intensive and El Niño vulnerabilities can impact food productivity.

Agricultural districts in the region use water from upstream Karnataka region and a weak southwest monsoon means less water inflows down south. Interior districts depend on rain-fed farming and small reservoirs or lakes, and when seasonal rainfall is unpredictable and local reservoirs of water are not well maintained and full, farming suffers.

Many regions in Tamil Nadu also rely heavily on groundwater and over-exploit them for agriculture but this water source is also getting depleted and struggling to recharge. Experts say that during El Niño there can be low rainfall days as well as short periods of intense rainfall. Intense rainfall does not help to recharge groundwater aquifers as water tends to run off instead of slowly percolating the soil and recharging them. According to the Central Ground Water Board’s 2025 assessment estimates, of the state’s 313 groundwater assessment units, 103 are classified as “over-exploited.”

Tamil Nadu has the second longest coastline in India of nearly 1,076 kilometres spanning 14 coastal districts. Coastal aquifers here are impacted by seawater intrusion due to sea level rise. This makes these areas more prone to drought conditions.

The Tamil Nadu Government constituted an expert committee in July, under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, to advise the Tamil Nadu Disaster Risk Reduction Agency (TNDRRA) on preparedness for El Niño.

“As El Niño disrupts the predictable monsoon, Tamil Nadu may experience both intense drought and severe deluge,” explains Nambi Appadurai, the Director of Climate Resilience Practice at World Resources Institute India, and a part of the expert committee. “Adapting to this erratic cycle in the agricultural context, demands a shift from reactive

analysis.tldr: Severe weather patterns could hurt crop harvests in Tamil Nadu, potentially pushing up local food prices and straining rural incomes.
the_story: The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) confirmed an 80-100% probability of an El Niño weather pattern extending to April 2027.
The southwest monsoon ended on September 30 with a 12.6% rainfall deficiency, reducing reservoir inflows from upstream Karnataka and the Western Ghats.
The Central Ground Water Board's 2025 assessment notes that 103 out of 313 groundwater units in Tamil Nadu are over-exploited.
Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU) projects normal rainfall of 468 mm for the northeast monsoon, but warns of uneven distribution causing dry conditions inland and intense rain on the coast.
The Tamil Nadu government formed an expert committee in July under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, to prepare for El Niño impacts.
analysis.what_happened: Climate change and warming ocean temperatures are driving a prolonged El Niño cycle, which disrupts normal monsoon rains. For Tamil Nadu, this has resulted in a weak southwest monsoon and unpredictable rainfall patterns, straining water reserves, agriculture, and groundwater levels.
analysis.analogy: It is like relying on a fixed monthly paycheck to fill your water tank and water your garden, but the schedule becomes totally erratic—some months bring a flood that spills over without soaking the soil, and other months bring nothing at all.
why_it_matters_india: El Niño reduces rainfall and depletes reservoir inflows from the Western Ghats and Karnataka.
Lower water availability harms major crops like paddy, groundnut, maize, pulses, and sugarcane.
Declining crop yields reduce farm incomes and local food supplies.
Reduced local food supplies can push up consumer food inflation for everyday items.

impacts.rationale: Lower crop yields in major agricultural states like Tamil Nadu can reduce supply and raise food prices, which is bad for household budgets.

impacts.target: Agri-input and consumer goods stocks in India
impacts.rationale: Stressed rural incomes and poor harvests typically lead to lower spending on goods and farming supplies, hurting company revenues.

watch_next: Updates on the actual rainfall distribution during the ongoing northeast monsoon season
Actions taken by the Tamil Nadu expert committee on disaster management
analysis.caveats: Localized heavy rainfall in coastal areas could offset some dryness, depending on how the northeast monsoon progresses in the coming weeks.

events.headline: How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain

items.title: How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang attends a summit at the Institute of Peace on October 8, 2026 in Washington, DC.

events.article_text:
Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, days after he admitted to having an affair with a Chinese data center executive, whom the U.S. intelligence agency believed to be a Chinese government agent. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive.

Nvidia’s board said that chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as the company’s interim chief executive until a permanent successor has been named.

Huang’s exit has triggered worries about Nvidia’s future as the world’s top chipmaker, and about the entire AI industry where Nvidia has been a hardware provider, an investor, and a community leader. Repercussions from the saga will impact China, which has yet to replace Nvidia chips with domestic alternatives, as well as Taiwan and South Korea, which host a vast network of Nvidia suppliers.

Here are the key questions emerging from Huang’s dramatic downfall.

Jensen Huang had been the biggest advocate for selling chips to China, which he argued helps America maintain its market dominance.

Despite the U.S. banning the export of advanced Nvidia chips to China, Chinese companies have been trying to access chips remotely by working with data centers in Southeast Asia.

Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang had an affair, served as the executive of Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. The Information reported that Alice Huang helped move about 240,000 H100, H200 and some A100 chips into China. Her companies also invested in DeepSeek, promising to supply Nvidia chips.

The Nvidia scandal will likely lead the U.S. government to tighten chip controls. Anticipating a crackdown, Chinese AI labs are trying to lock in overseas supplies of Nvidia chips, while traders in China are stockpiling restricted chips, Reuters reported.

Chinese chips are catching up in performance, but Nvidia chips are still essential to the AI industry.

In the first half of the year, Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China, down 44% from a year earlier and making up 34% of the market, according to a Reuters report, citing IDC data. In the same period, leading Chinese chipmaker HuaweiiHuaweiHuawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions.READ MORE shipped 572,000 ‌AI ⁠accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, accounting for 28% of the market,

AlibabaiAlibabaAlibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall.READ MORE’s chip unit T-Head had 7% of the market, followed by Cambricon’s 5%. BaiduiBaiduBaidu is a Chinese technology company that operates the country’s biggest search engine and video-streaming service iQiyi.READ MORE subsidiary Kunlunxin held 4% and Hygon had 3%.

Although AI labs are increasingly working with chipmakers to make sure their models can run on domestic infrastructure, most AI developers still train new models on Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s B300 delivers 6.75 times the arithmetic performance of Huawei’s best Ascend 950 chip, according to research firm Epoch AI. Huawei also lags behind Nvidia in production volume.

Jensen Huang enjoys rock star status across Asia, especially in his birth country Taiwan, where he would visit night markets, share snacks with fans, and host banquets with executives of Taiwanese suppliers. He said the company planned to invest $150 billion a year in Taiwan.

Many internet users expressed disappointment that they lost a role model in tech. Some wrote that the spy allegations and the criticisms of Huang would add to the discrimination of Asians working in America’s tech industry.

Huang’s departure is also creating uncertainty around Nvidia’s supply chain relationship with Asian companies. But several executives at Nvidia’s Taiwanese suppliers said they still expected steady orders from Nvidia in the coming years because of the sustained demand from the AI industry, according to Taiwan’s Central News Agency.

Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.

A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.

MinoHealth researchers in Ghana jailbroke their own LLM as a test. What emerged were thousands of toxin recipes—and an urgent push for regulation.

analysis.tldr: The sudden departure of Nvidia's boss could trigger stricter US rules on selling advanced chips, shaking up global tech supply chains that Indian software and technology firms rely on.
the_story: Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday following admissions of an affair with a Chinese data center executive whom US intelligence suspected of being a government agent.
Nvidia appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive while it searches for a permanent successor.
Reports revealed that Alice Huang, the executive connected to the affair, helped move roughly 240,000 restricted Nvidia chips into China via a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed.

In the first half of the year, Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators [specialized computer chips used to build artificial intelligence] in China, capturing 34% of the market, while Chinese rival Huawei shipped 572,000 units.
Despite the leadership exit, executives at Nvidia's Taiwanese suppliers expect steady ongoing orders due to high global demand for AI hardware.
analysis.what_happened: Nvidia's top boss stepped down after admitting to an affair with a Chinese executive linked to security concerns, which involved the illicit transfer of advanced AI chips into China. This crisis has plunged the world's leading chipmaker into uncertainty and raised fears of immediate regulatory crackdowns by the US government.
analysis.analogy: It is like the star captain of a global cargo shipping company suddenly getting sidelined due to a security breach, leaving the whole fleet scrambling for permits while competitors rush to fill the gap.
why_it_matters_india: US chip rules tighten -> US regulators restrict high-end tech exports further.
Global tech supply chains wobble -> Component costs for global software and AI tools shift.
Indian IT companies (which build applications on top of global AI hardware) face changing software development costs.
Investor sentiment shifts -> Global tech stock volatility impacts Indian technology shares and broader market confidence.

impacts.rationale: Sudden leadership loss and potential regulatory probes create uncertainty, which typically drives investors away in the short term.
Broader global tech sector jitters can spill over into Indian outsourcing firms, which is generally bad for short-term stock performance.
Global tech sell-offs can create minor ripples across emerging market equities, causing mild friction for local investors.

watch_next: Official US government announcements regarding tighter semiconductor export controls
Updates from Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress on future hardware production plans
analysis.caveats: If Nvidia's board names a strong permanent successor quickly, the panic over supply chain disruptions could fade faster than expected.

events.headline: 15 Arab and Islamic countries welcome united kingdom , Australia sanctions against Israeli settlement activities

items.title: 15 Arab and Islamic countries welcome united kingdom , Australia sanctions against Israeli settlement activities

events.article_text:
Amman [Jordan], November 20 (ANI): Fifteen Arab and Islamic countries have welcomed the decisions of the United Kingdom and Australia to impose sanctions in response to Israeli settlement activities in the occupied West Bank, calling for greater international accountability against entities and individuals involved in settlement expansion and annexation policies.

In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Pakistan, Trkiye, Algeria, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Kuwait, Libya, Maldives, Egypt and Niger expressed support for international measures, including sanctions, against those responsible for settlement activities in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

The ministers also welcomed the United Kingdom's decision to impose sanctions on an organisation accused of obstructing the delivery of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip.

The joint statement said the ministers 'express support for all efforts to ensure accountability, including through appropriate international measures and the imposition of sanctions on entities and individuals responsible for settlement activities, including the E1 settlement plan, as well as those that support, facilitate or implement settlement expansion and annexation policies'.

The ministers reiterated their strongest condemnation of Israel's continued settlement policies in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, particularly the E1 settlement plan and related settlement activities east of occupied East Jerusalem. They also expressed hope that the decisions taken by the UK and Australia would encourage other members of the international community to follow suit.

According to the joint statement, the ministers considered the measures taken by the UK and Australia to be in line with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions, including United Nations Security Council Resolution 2334 (2016), as well as the Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice dated July 19, 2024.

The statement further underlined the obligation of all states not to recognise as legal the situation arising from Israel's unlawful occupation or render aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by the occupation.

'In this regard, they reiterate their call for Israel to rescind all measures taken in connection with settlement activities and other measures aimed at altering the geographic and demographic character of the Occupied Palestinian Territory,' the ministry statement said.

The foreign ministers also condemned the Israeli military escalation in Gaza and called for the full and immediate implementation of US President Donald Trump's Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict.

According to the statement, the implementation of the plan is necessary to ensure security and stability, address the humanitarian situation, facilitate reconstruction and recovery, and lay the foundations for lasting peace.

The ministers further underscored that Gaza is an integral part of the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

Emphasising the need for a political resolution to the conflict, the statement said that the only viable path towards achieving a just, lasting and comprehensive peace was the implementation of the two-State solution.

The ministers called for the establishment of an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable Palestinian State based on the June 4, 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital, in accordance with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions. (ANI)

analysis.tldr: Political actions in the Middle East have little direct impact on your daily expenses in India, unless broader conflicts flare up and push up global fuel prices.
the_story: Fifteen Arab and Islamic countries, including Jordan, the UAE, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia, welcomed sanctions by the United Kingdom and Australia against Israeli settlement activities in the West Bank.
The UK also placed sanctions on an organization accused of blocking humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip.
The foreign ministers from these 15 nations called for more international accountability against groups and individuals expanding settlements and annexation policies.
The ministers condemned Israel's military escalation in Gaza and called for the full implementation of a plan proposed by US President Donald Trump to end the conflict.
The joint statement reaffirmed support for a two-state solution, aiming for an independent Palestinian state based on June 4, 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital.
analysis.what_happened: Fifteen Arab and Islamic nations issued a joint statement praising recent UK and Australia sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The move was driven by a shared push from these countries for international penalties against policies expanding Israeli settlements and blocking aid in Gaza.
analysis.analogy: It is like neighbors in an apartment building formally backing a penalty levied against one tenant by the building management, hoping it forces a change in behavior.
why_it_matters_india: Diplomatic statements from Middle Eastern and Western nations show ongoing international friction over the conflict.
Increased geopolitical tensions can sometimes trigger worries about oil supply disruptions in the Middle East.
If oil supplies look threatened, global crude oil prices can rise.
Higher oil prices make imports costlier for India, potentially raising domestic inflation (the rising cost of everyday goods) and weakening the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars).

impacts.rationale: Diplomatic statements alone rarely shift oil markets unless they spark actual supply disruptions, making costlier fuel unlikely for now.
Global investors buy safe-haven assets like gold when Middle East tensions escalate, making jewellery and investment gold pricier for Indian buyers.
A weaker rupee makes imported goods like electronics and oil more expensive for everyday Indians.

watch_next: Whether other Western countries follow the UK and Australia in imposing sanctions
Any signs of actual supply disruptions or military escalation affecting regional oil shipping lanes
analysis.caveats: This news is purely diplomatic and regulatory, so it carries almost no immediate financial impact on Indian markets unless it triggers a wider regional conflict.

history.title: The embargo that rewired the world economy
history.what: Arab oil producers cut output and embargoed several countries during the Yom Kippur war. Oil went from about $3 a barrel to $12 within months, and the industrial world discovered how completely it depended on a resource it did not control.
history.why: Oil demand had grown for two decades on the assumption of permanently cheap supply, so there was no spare capacity and no stockpile anywhere. The producers realised they had collective pricing power and used it. A political event became an economic one because no buffer existed.
history.impact: Stagflation — high inflation and high unemployment together, which economists had thought nearly impossible. US shares fell about 48%. Petrol rationing across the West. For oil-importing India, the import bill and inflation both surged.
history.policy: Strategic petroleum reserves were created so a political shock could not immediately become a price shock. Fuel-efficiency standards were imposed on cars. Nuclear and, much later, renewable programmes were accelerated. The International Energy Agency was founded to coordinate responses.
history.consequence: Rich-world oil consumption per unit of output has more than halved since. The reserves and efficiency rules genuinely worked, which is why later oil shocks — including 2022 — hurt considerably less than 1973 did.
history.pattern: A concentrated supply of something essential is a standing political risk, whatever the price chart says. The response is always the same — build a buffer, use less, find alternatives — and it takes about a decade to work.
history.india_echo: India imports over 85% of its crude, so this is the permanent structural weakness behind the rupee, inflation and the current account deficit. It is also why India's solar push and its own strategic reserve are macro stories, not environmental ones.
history.watch_for: Any critical input where a handful of countries control most of the supply. Rare earths, advanced chips and lithium are today's version of the question.
